paper.title: Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Net: Selective Forgetting in Deep Networks
paper.source_of_truth: arXiv LaTeX e-print (arxiv.org/e-print/1911.04933); math cataloged from main.tex; the rendered PDF was used to fix equation numbers and the appendix letter (the proofs are Appendix C).
paper.scope_note: This is a methods paper. Its self-contained, provable mathematical content is four propositions and one lemma, collected in Appendix C ('Proofs'). Three of them (Lemma 1, Proposition 1, Proposition 2) are information-theoretic inequalities that all rest on the log-sum inequality; Proposition 3 is a linear-algebra identity about two quadratic gradient flows; Proposition 4 is a matrix optimization that rests on an explicit second-order (Gaussian/quadratic) approximation stated in its own hypotheses. The Fisher-information approximation of the Hessian (Sec. 3.3, Eq. (8)), the deep-network scrubbing algorithm, and the variational bound of Sec. 4 are design/approximation choices, not theorems, and are not part of this catalog.

items.label: Lemma 1
items.name: KL divergence between weight distributions contracts under any readout function

human.statement: Sec. 2 'Definition and Testing of Forgetting', Lemma 1

background_notation.w: the weights of a trained model
background_notation.S(w): the (stochastic) scrubbing function applied to the weights
background_notation.S_0(w): the certificate scrubbing function, not depending on the forgetting set
background_notation.D: the full training set; D_r its retained part
background_notation.f: an arbitrary readout function applied to the weights
background_notation.P(S(w)|D): the distribution of scrubbed weights after training on D

hypotheses: f is an arbitrary (measurable) function of the weights.
The proof is given for discrete random variables (stated in the paper).
items.statement_informal: Applying a readout function f to the weights can only decrease the KL divergence between the scrubbed distribution and its certificate. Hence controlling the KL on the full weights guarantees robustness against every readout an attacker might use.
items.statement_formal: For any function f, KL( P(f(S(w))|D) || P(f(S_0(w))|D_r) ) <= KL( P(S(w)|D) || P(S_0(w)|D_r) ).
items.proof_as_in_paper: Write Q(w)=P(S(w)|D) and R(w)=P(S_0(w)|D_r) and prove KL(Q(f(w))||R(f(w))) <= KL(Q(w)||R(w)). Let W_c = { w : f(w)=c }, so Q(f(w)=c)=sum_{w in W_c} Q(w) and R(f(w)=c)=sum_{w in W_c} R(w). Then KL(Q(f(w))||R(f(w))) = sum_c Q(f(w)=c) log [ Q(f(w)=c) / R(f(w)=c) ] = sum_c ( sum_{w in W_c} Q(w) ) log [ ( sum_{w in W_c} Q(w) ) / ( sum_{w in W_c} R(w) ) ]  (Eq. (9)), while KL(Q(w)||R(w)) = sum_c sum_{w in W_c} Q(w) log ( Q(w)/R(w) )  (Eq. (10)). By the log-sum inequality, for each c, ( sum_{w in W_c} Q(w) ) log [ ( sum_{w in W_c} Q(w) ) / ( sum_{w in W_c} R(w) ) ] <= sum_{w in W_c} Q(w) log ( Q(w)/R(w) ). Summing over all c concludes the proof.
items.proof_technique: Log-sum inequality applied fiberwise over the level sets of f, then summed.
items.proof_completeness: self-contained given the log-sum inequality (used as a standard result).
external_dependencies: Log-sum inequality: for nonnegative a_i and positive b_i, ( sum_i a_i ) log ( ( sum_i a_i ) / ( sum_i b_i ) ) <= sum_i a_i log ( a_i / b_i ). Consequence of the convexity of t |-> t log t.
known_issues_in_paper: The proof writes R(w) = P(S_0(w)|D_{-k}), using D_{-k} (the data without class k) for the retained set that the statement calls D_r; D_{-k} is a special case of D_r. Notation only.

In Eq. (10) the rewrite of KL(Q||R) is printed sum_c sum_{w in W_c} log(Q(w)/R(w)), dropping the leading weight Q(w); the correct expression, used in the proof and needed for the log-sum step, is sum_c sum_{w in W_c} Q(w) log(Q(w)/R(w)).
items.formalization_notes: Model a discrete distribution over a Fintype alpha as Q : alpha -> R with Q nonnegative. Define klDiv Q R = sum_x Q x * log (Q x / R x). The readout f : alpha -> beta pushes Q forward to Qf c = sum_{x, f x = c} Q x. The statement is klDiv Qf Rf <= klDiv Q R, obtained by proving the log-sum inequality as a helper lemma (from convexity of t log t) and summing it over the fibers of f.

lean.route_note: Proved fiberwise from the self-contained log_sum_inequality (Basic.lean), then recombined with Finset.sum_fiberwise, faithful to the paper's per-level-set argument.

items.label: Proposition 2 (Local Forgetting Bound)
items.name: KL of the seed-averaged distributions is bounded by the seed-averaged KL

human.statement: Sec. 2.1 'Stability and Local Forgetting Bound', Proposition 2

background_notation.epsilon: the random seed of the training algorithm A(D, epsilon)
background_notation.P(S(w)|D, epsilon): the scrubbed-weight distribution for a fixed seed
background_notation.P(S(w)|D): the seed-averaged distribution, E_epsilon[ P(S(w)|D, epsilon) ]

hypotheses: The training algorithm A(D, epsilon) is deterministic given the data and the seed epsilon ~ P(epsilon).
P(S(w)|D) = E_epsilon[ P(S(w)|D, epsilon) ] (and likewise for S_0, D_r).
The proof is given for discrete random variables.
items.statement_informal: The KL divergence between the two seed-averaged (mixture) distributions is no larger than the average, over seeds, of the per-seed KL divergences. This lets one bound a hard-to-estimate mixture KL by an average of simple per-seed KLs.
items.statement_formal: With Q(w) = E_epsilon[ Q(w|epsilon) ] and R(w) = E_epsilon[ R(w|epsilon) ], KL( P(S(w)|D) || P(S_0(w)|D_r) ) <= E_epsilon[ KL( P(S(w)|D, epsilon) || P(S_0(w)|D_r, epsilon) ) ].
items.proof_as_in_paper: Write Q(w)=P(S(w)|D), R(w)=P(S_0(w)|D_r). Then KL(Q(w)||R(w)) = integral Q(w) log (Q(w)/R(w)) dw = integral E_epsilon[Q(w|epsilon)] log ( E_epsilon[Q(w|epsilon)] / E_epsilon[R(w|epsilon)] ) dw <= integral E_epsilon[ Q(w|epsilon) log ( Q(w|epsilon)/R(w|epsilon) ) ] dw = E_epsilon[ integral Q(w|epsilon) log ( Q(w|epsilon)/R(w|epsilon) ) dw ] = E_epsilon[ KL(Q(w|epsilon)||R(w|epsilon)) ], where the inequality is the log-sum inequality (convexity) applied for each w over the seed distribution.
items.proof_technique: Log-sum inequality applied per outcome over the seed index (joint convexity of KL divergence).
known_issues_in_paper: In the transcribed proof R(w) is written as P(S(w)|D_r); it denotes the certificate P(S_0(w)|D_r) as in the statement. A couple of the intermediate log-ratios write P(w|epsilon) for R(w|epsilon). Notation only.
items.formalization_notes: Model the seed as a finite index type sigma with a probability weight p : sigma -> R (nonnegative, summing to one). Given families Q, R : sigma -> alpha -> R of discrete distributions, the mixtures are Qbar x = sum_e p e * Q e x. The statement is klDiv Qbar Rbar <= sum_e p e * klDiv (Q e) (R e), obtained from the same log-sum inequality helper applied for each x over the seed index e.

lean.route_note: Formalized as the discrete mixture over a finite seed distribution p (the discrete analogue of the paper's E_epsilon, consistent with the paper's own 'consider the random variables to be discrete'); the log-sum inequality is applied per outcome over the seed index, then the sums are swapped.

items.name: Bound on the Shannon information a readout extracts about the forgetting cohort
items.label: Proposition 1 / Eq. (2)

human.statement: Sec. 2 'Definition and Testing of Forgetting', Proposition 1, Eq. (2)

background_notation.D_f: the forgetting cohort, treated here as a random variable
background_notation.Y: an attribute of interest that depends on D_f
background_notation.I(X; Z): Shannon mutual information, E_x[ KL( p(z|x) || p(z) ) ]
background_notation.f(S(w)): a readout applied to the scrubbed weights

hypotheses: The forgetting set D_f is a random variable; Y depends on D_f.
The retained set D_r is fixed (deterministic).
Markov chain Y <- D_f -> w -> S(w) -> f(S(w)); in particular Y and f(S(w)) are conditionally independent given D_f.
The proof is given for discrete random variables.
items.statement_informal: The amount of Shannon information that the readout of the scrubbed weights carries about any attribute Y of the forgetting cohort is upper bounded by the expected KL forgetting quantity. Thus driving the KL to zero drives to zero the information any attribute leaks.
items.proof_as_in_paper: From the Markov chain Y <- D_f -> w -> S(w) -> f(S(w)), the Data Processing Inequality gives I(Y; f(S(w))) <= I(D_f; f(S(w))). Bound the right-hand side: I(D_f; f(S(w))) = E_{D_f}[ KL( p(f(S(w))|D_f ∪ D_r) || p(f(S(w))) ) ] = E_{D_f} E_{p(f(S(w))|D_f ∪ D_r)}[ log ( p(f(S(w))|D_f ∪ D_r) / p(f(S_0(w))|D_r) ) + log ( p(f(S_0(w))|D_r) / p(f(S(w))) ) ] = E_{D_f}[ KL( p(f(S(w))|D_f ∪ D_r) || p(f(S_0(w))|D_r) ) ] - KL( p(f(S_0(w))) || p(f(S(w))|D_r) ) <= E_{D_f}[ KL( p(f(S(w))|D_f ∪ D_r) || p(f(S_0(w))|D_r) ) ], the last inequality because KL divergence is nonnegative.
items.proof_technique: Data Processing Inequality for mutual information over the Markov chain, then a variational upper bound on mutual information (add and subtract a reference distribution and drop a nonnegative KL term).
items.proof_completeness: self-contained given the Data Processing Inequality (used as a standard result) and the nonnegativity of KL.
external_dependencies: Data Processing Inequality for Shannon mutual information over a Markov chain.
known_issues_in_paper: The subtracted term is written KL( p(f(S_0(w))) || p(f(S(w))|D_r) ); this is the nonnegative KL of the reference identity I(X;Z) = E_x[ KL( p(z|x) || q(z) ) ] - KL( p(z) || q(z) ), whose reference-distribution arguments are stated somewhat loosely. The bound (drop a nonnegative KL) is correct.
items.formalization_notes: Discrete finite model. Mutual information I(X; Z) = sum_{x} pX x * klDiv (pZgivenX x) pZ. The variational-bound half follows from nonnegativity of klDiv (any reference q gives I(X;Z) <= E_x[ klDiv (p(z|x)) q ]). The Data Processing Inequality half is derived from the same log-sum-inequality machinery / chain rule of mutual information (or Mathlib's information-theory API if it provides mutual info and DPI). Decide the exact route when proving.

added_hypotheses: The Data Processing Inequality I(Y; f(S(w))) <= I(D_f; f(S(w))) is taken as a hypothesis (hDPI in information_bound), exactly as the paper invokes it as a standard result.
The variational bound is proved for an arbitrary reference distribution q; the paper's q = P(f(S_0(w))|D_r) is one instance.
lean.route_note: The substantive step, I(X;Z) <= E_x[KL(p(z|x)||q)] with gap exactly KL(marginal||q) >= 0, is proved in full from Gibbs' inequality (klDiv_nonneg, Basic.lean). information_bound then chains the hypothesized DPI.

items.label: Proposition 3 (Optimal Quadratic Scrubbing)
items.name: A deterministic map sends the D-trained gradient flow exactly onto the D_r-trained gradient flow

background_notation.L_D, L_{D_r}: the (quadratic) losses on the full and retained sets
background_notation.A: the Hessian of L_D; B: the Hessian of L_{D_r}
background_notation.w_A^*, w_B^*: the minimizers of L_D and L_{D_r}
background_notation.A_t(D, epsilon): the gradient-flow training path at time t, from random initialization w_0 = epsilon
background_notation.d: w_A(t) - w_A^* = A^{-1} grad L_D(w_A(t)); d_r: w_A(t) - w_B^* = B^{-1} grad L_{D_r}(w_A(t))

hypotheses: L_D(w) = (1/2)(w - w_A^*)^T A (w - w_A^*) and L_{D_r}(w) = (1/2)(w - w_B^*)^T B (w - w_B^*) are quadratic, with A, B symmetric positive definite.
Training is the gradient flow of the loss from initialization w_0, giving the closed forms w_A(t) = w_A^* + exp(-At)(w_0 - w_A^*) and w_B(t) = w_B^* + exp(-Bt)(w_0 - w_B^*) (the same w_0 for both).
items.statement_informal: Under quadratic losses trained by gradient flow, a single deterministic map h carries the model trained on all of D exactly onto the model that gradient flow would have produced on D_r alone, for every random initialization and every time. In particular this scrubs all information about D_f. As training converges (t to infinity) the map reduces to the Newton update S_infinity(w) = w - B^{-1} grad L_{D_r}(w).
items.statement_formal: Let h(w) = w + exp(-Bt) exp(At) d + exp(-Bt)(d_r - d) - d_r. Then h(A_t(D, epsilon)) = A_t(D_r, epsilon) for all initializations epsilon and all times t. As t -> infinity this reduces to S_infinity(w) = w - B^{-1} grad L_{D_r}(w).
items.proof_as_in_paper: With L_D, L_{D_r} quadratic, the gradient flow paths solve wdot = -A(w - w_A^*) and wdot = -B(w - w_B^*), giving w_A(t) = w_A^* + exp(-At)(w_0 - w_A^*) and w_B(t) = w_B^* + exp(-Bt)(w_0 - w_B^*). From the first, w_0 = exp(At)(w_A(t) - w_A^*) + w_A^* = exp(At) d_A + w_A^*, with d_A := w_A(t) - w_A^* = A^{-1} grad L_D(w_A(t)). Substituting into the second and writing d_B := w_A(t) - w_B^* = B^{-1} grad L_{D_r}(w_A(t)): w_B(t) = exp(-Bt) exp(At) d_A + exp(-Bt)(w_A^* - w_B^*) + w_B^* = w_A(t) + exp(-Bt) exp(At) d_A + exp(-Bt)(d_B - d_A) - d_B. Identifying d = d_A, d_r = d_B gives h(w_A(t)) = w_B(t).
items.proof_technique: Solve the two linear (quadratic-loss) gradient flows in closed form and eliminate the shared initialization w_0; the only property of the matrix exponential used is that exp(At) is the inverse of exp(-At).
external_dependencies: Closed-form solution of the linear ODE wdot = -M(w - w^*), namely w(t) = w^* + exp(-Mt)(w_0 - w^*), and exp(Mt) exp(-Mt) = I.
known_issues_in_paper: In the stated map h (main text, appendix, and Eq. (6)) the middle term reads exp(-Bt)(d - d_r); the proof's own final line derives exp(-Bt)(d_r - d). The identity h(A_t(D)) = A_t(D_r) holds with the sign exp(-Bt)(d_r - d); with the printed sign it holds only when d = d_r. (The t -> infinity Newton update Eq. (7) is unaffected, since this term vanishes.)
The appendix restatement of h drops the leading 'w +' present in the main-text statement and in Eq. (6); the proof confirms the 'w' term is present.
The proof writes the gradient-flow ODE as wdot = A(w - w^*); the gradient flow is wdot = -grad L = -A(w - w^*). The stated solution exp(-At) already carries the sign; only the ODE line omits it.
The proof writes L_{D_f}(w) = (1/2)(w - w_B^*)^T B (w - w_B^*) with B = Hessian of L_{D_r}; since B is the retained-set Hessian this quadratic is L_{D_r}, not L_{D_f}.
items.formalization_notes: Formalize the pure algebraic identity relating the two closed-form flows, using the corrected middle-term sign exp(-Bt)(d_r - d). The matrix exponential enters only through invertibility (exp(At) exp(-At) = I), so exp(-At) can either be Matrix.exp (faithful to the statement) used via its inverse, or an abstract invertible matrix. Define A_t(D, epsilon) and A_t(D_r, epsilon) by the paper's own closed forms (the paper states 'the training path is the solution ... which is given respectively by ...').

added_hypotheses: The two gradient-flow paths are given by their closed forms (the paper's own 'which is given respectively by' step), not re-derived from an ODE-existence theorem.
e^{At} inverts e^{-At} (FA * EA = 1); in quadratic_scrubbing_flow_identity_exp this is discharged from the genuine matrix exponential via exp(MA)*exp(-MA) = exp(0) = 1.
The formalized map uses the corrected middle-term sign e^{-Bt}(d_r - d) that the paper's proof derives (see known_issues_in_paper).
lean.route_note: Proves the algebraic flow substitution identity h(w_A(t)) = w_B(t), which is the content of the paper's proof. The t -> infinity Newton update (Eq. (7)) is NOT formalized: it is an analytic limit (e^{-Bt} -> 0) the paper takes informally; only the finite-t identity that it specializes is proved.

items.label: Proposition 4 (Robust Scrubbing Procedure)
items.name: Optimal noise covariance minimizing the (approximated) Forgetting Lagrangian

background_notation.h(w): a deterministic scrubbing map; w' the target weights trained on D_r
background_notation.Sigma_h: covariance of the residual error h(w) - w' ~ N(0, Sigma_h)
background_notation.Sigma: the covariance of the added noise n ~ N(0, Sigma)
background_notation.B: the Hessian of L_{D_r} at the scrubbed weights, symmetric positive definite
background_notation.lambda: the positive trade-off weight of the Forgetting Lagrangian
background_notation.sigma_h^2: the isotropic residual variance when Sigma_h = sigma_h^2 I

hypotheses: h(w) - w' ~ N(0, Sigma_h) (normally distributed residual error).
L_{D_r}(w) is (locally) quadratic around h(w), with Hessian B symmetric positive definite; the loss is replaced by its second-order approximation (the paper's stated approximation, dropping o(n^2)).
The scrubbing has the form S(w) = h(w) + n with n ~ N(0, Sigma), Sigma symmetric positive definite.
items.statement_informal: Among noise covariances Sigma, the one that minimizes the (second-order approximated) Forgetting Lagrangian solves Sigma B Sigma = lambda Sigma_h. When the residual error is isotropic, Sigma_h = sigma_h^2 I, the optimum is Sigma = sqrt(lambda sigma_h^2) B^{-1/2}.
items.statement_formal: Under the stated Gaussian/quadratic approximation the Forgetting Lagrangian reduces to L(Sigma) = L_{D_r}(h(w)) + (1/2) tr(B Sigma) + (lambda/2) tr(Sigma^{-1} Sigma_h). Its minimizer over symmetric positive definite Sigma satisfies Sigma B Sigma = lambda Sigma_h. In the isotropic case Sigma_h = sigma_h^2 I the minimizer is Sigma = sqrt(lambda sigma_h^2) B^{-1/2}.
items.proof_as_in_paper: Second-order expansion of the retain loss: E_{n ~ N(0, Sigma)}[ L_{D_r}(h(w) + n) ] = E_n[ L_{D_r}(h(w)) + grad L_{D_r}(h(w))^T Sigma^{1/2} n + (1/2)(Sigma^{1/2} n)^T B (Sigma^{1/2} n) + o(n^2) ] ~= L_{D_r}(h(w)) + (1/2) E_n[ (Sigma^{1/2} n)^T B (Sigma^{1/2} n) ] = L_{D_r}(h(w)) + (1/2) tr(B Sigma) (the linear term vanishes since E[n] = 0). For the KL term, with S_0(w) = w + n', n' ~ N(0, Sigma), so P(S_0(w)|D_r, epsilon) ~ N(w, Sigma): E_epsilon[ KL( P(S(w)|D, epsilon) || P(S_0(w)|D_r, epsilon) ) ] = (1/2) E_epsilon[ (h(w) - w')^T Sigma^{-1} (h(w) - w') ] = (1/2) tr(Sigma^{-1} Sigma_h), using h(w) - w' ~ N(0, Sigma_h). Combining, L = L_{D_r}(h(w)) + (1/2) tr(B Sigma) + (1/2) tr(Sigma^{-1} Sigma_h). Setting grad_Sigma L = 0 gives the optimality condition Sigma B Sigma = lambda Sigma_h; if Sigma_h = sigma_h^2 I this simplifies to Sigma = sqrt(lambda sigma_h^2) B^{-1/2}.
items.proof_technique: Gaussian second-order approximation of the loss (E[n^T M n] = tr(M Sigma)), then minimize a trace objective in Sigma via a first-order stationarity condition.
items.proof_completeness: self-contained modulo the stated second-order (Gaussian/quadratic) approximation; the optimization of the resulting approximated Lagrangian is exact.
external_dependencies: Gaussian second-moment identity E_{n ~ N(0, Sigma)}[ n^T M n ] = tr(M Sigma).
Matrix-derivative identities grad_Sigma tr(B Sigma) = B and grad_Sigma tr(Sigma^{-1} Sigma_h) = -Sigma^{-1} Sigma_h Sigma^{-1} (used by the paper's first-order condition).
known_issues_in_paper: In the KL-term line the second factor is printed (h(w) - h(w')); it should be (h(w) - w') for the expression to equal (1/2) tr(Sigma^{-1} Sigma_h) via h(w) - w' ~ N(0, Sigma_h).
The statement writes B = Hessian of L_{D_r}(k); the argument should be w (or h(w)), as in the main text. k is the class label.
items.formalization_notes: Formalize the isotropic case as a GLOBAL minimum via completing the square, which needs no matrix calculus and is stronger than the paper's first-order stationarity. With c = lambda sigma_h^2, minimize g(Sigma) = (1/2) tr(B Sigma) + (c/2) tr(Sigma^{-1}) over symmetric positive definite Sigma. Setting P = B^{1/2} Sigma^{1/2}, Q = sqrt(c) Sigma^{-1/2}: tr(P^T P) = tr(B Sigma), tr(Q^T Q) = c tr(Sigma^{-1}), and tr(P^T Q) = sqrt(c) tr(B^{1/2}) is constant. From tr((P - Q)^T (P - Q)) >= 0, tr(B Sigma) + c tr(Sigma^{-1}) >= 2 sqrt(c) tr(B^{1/2}), with equality iff P = Q iff Sigma = sqrt(c) B^{-1/2}. Also verify directly that Sigma^* = sqrt(lambda sigma_h^2) B^{-1/2} satisfies the paper's optimality condition Sigma^* B Sigma^* = lambda sigma_h^2 I = lambda Sigma_h. Ingredients: Matrix.PosSemidef square roots, tr(M^T M) >= 0, cyclic trace. The underlying second-order approximation (the reduced objective) is a stated hypothesis, not re-derived.

added_hypotheses: The second-order (Gaussian/quadratic) approximation of the Forgetting Lagrangian is taken as the paper's own stated hypothesis: the objective is the reduced trace form (1/2)tr(B Sigma) + (lambda sigma_h^2 / 2) tr(Sigma^{-1}), not re-derived.
The isotropic case Sigma_h = sigma_h^2 I (the paper's 'In particular, if the error is isotropic'), with c = lambda sigma_h^2.

Symmetric square roots Bsqrt, Ssqrt of B and Sigma are taken as hypotheses (Bsqrt*Bsqrt = B, Ssqrt*Ssqrt = Sigma); every real PD matrix has a unique PD (hence symmetric) square root by the spectral theorem, so the hypotheses are satisfiable for exactly the matrices in the paper's scope. They are not constructed via the continuous functional calculus.
Invertibility of the square roots (IsUnit det), automatic for PD matrices.
lean.route_note: Proves the GLOBAL optimum by completing the square in the trace inner product (two_mul_trace_le_of_transpose), strictly stronger than the paper's first-order stationarity via matrix calculus. robust_scrubbing_isotropic_bound is a universal lower bound over all PD Sigma; robust_scrubbing_isotropic_attains shows Sigma* = sqrt(c) B^{-1/2} attains it (hence a global minimizer); robust_scrubbing_isotropic_optimality_condition verifies the paper's condition Sigma B Sigma = lambda Sigma_h (= c I isotropic).
